prompt: When the recommendations service gets slow, product pages wait on it and the whole site's threads pile up.
why: Trip the breaker after repeated timeouts; render pages without recommendations until it recovers.
trap: Rate limiting protects a service from its callers; here the caller needs protecting from the service.

prompt: One failing downstream service caused a cascading failure across five upstream services last week.
why: Breakers fail fast so callers stop tying up resources on a dead dependency.
trap: Queues help with async work, but these are synchronous calls.

prompt: A shipping-rate API goes down briefly, and when it comes back, everyone's retries knock it over again.
why: An open breaker stops calls; half-open lets a trickle through to test recovery.
trap: Idempotency makes retries safe, not gentle.

prompt: A flaky third-party tax API times out a few times an hour, and each timeout blocks checkout for 30 seconds.
why: Short timeouts plus a breaker that falls back to an estimated tax when open.
trap: Caching works only if tax results repeat exactly.

prompt: When the inventory service is down, each product page waits 30 seconds for a timeout before showing an error.
why: After a few failures the breaker opens and calls fail immediately, so pages show a fallback fast.
trap: A shorter timeout helps, but the breaker stops calling at all.

prompt: After a dependency recovers, you want to let a few test requests through before sending full traffic again.
why: That's the half-open state: probe, then close the breaker if they succeed.
trap: Rate limiting caps traffic forever; half-open is a temporary probe.

prompt: If the personalization service fails, the homepage should show a generic list instead of an error, and stop calling it for a while.
tells: stop calling it for a while
why: A breaker plus fallback degrades gracefully.
trap: Caching could supply the fallback, but "stop calling for a while" is the breaker.

prompt: Calls to a slow payments partner tie up all 200 request threads, so even pages that don't need payments stop responding.
why: Trip a breaker (and isolate the call with its own pool) so one bad dependency can't starve everything.
trap: Adding servers just gives the slow partner more threads to tie up.
